pos: n. (delay; remissness — what scoffers mistake the Lord's longsuffering for)
etymology: From Old English slaec, loose or careless. At 2 Peter 3:9 it renders Greek bradutes, slowness — a word for tardiness, used of the only Person in Scripture ever accused of it.
biblical_def:
Peter has just quoted the scoffers of the last days — Where is the promise of his coming? — and answers them in one of the most carefully built sentences in the epistles: The Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness; but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance. The apostle does not deny the delay. He reinterprets it. What men count slackness is in fact longsuffering, and the delay has a purpose that the scoffers, by continuing to breathe, are themselves benefiting from.

Two supports hold the argument up. The first is the verse before: one day is with the Lord as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day. The complaint assumes that God keeps time the way we do, and He does not. The second is the verse further on, where Peter says the thing plainly: account that the longsuffering of our Lord is salvation. The interval is not an embarrassment to be explained away; it is the room in which the elect are gathered in. Every soul converted since the ascension has been converted inside the delay that the scoffers are complaining about, which means the question why has He not come? is answered for most Christians by their own existence. The word runs the other way too. Where God is not slack, men are, and Proverbs is unsparing: He becometh poor that dealeth with a slack hand.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): remissness; negligence; want of eagerness or diligence; slowness.
webster_full: SLACKNESS, n. Remissness; negligence; inattention; slowness; tardiness.
SLACK, a. Not tense; loose; remiss; not using due diligence; backward.
LONGSUFFERING, n. Bearing injuries or provocation for a long time; patient; not easily provoked.
REPENTANCE, n. Sorrow or deep contrition for sin, as an offense and dishonor to God, with a sincere purpose of amendment.
SCOFFER, n. One who scoffs; one who mocks, derides or reproaches.
scriptures: 2 Peter 3:9
The Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness; but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance.
2 Peter 3:8
But, beloved, be not ignorant of this one thing, that one day is with the Lord as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day.
2 Peter 3:15
And account that the longsuffering of our Lord is salvation; even as our beloved brother Paul also according to the wisdom given unto him hath written unto you;
Proverbs 10:4
He becometh poor that dealeth with a slack hand: but the hand of the diligent maketh rich.
corruption_summary: 2 Peter 3:9 is lifted out of its paragraph to deny particular redemption, when Peter's us-ward and any are the beloved he is writing to, not the scoffers he has just described.
corruption_paragraphs: No verse is quoted against the Reformed doctrine of election more often than this one, and the quotation almost always begins halfway through. Peter writes longsuffering to us-ward — to us, the beloved, whom he has addressed by that name three times in the chapter — and the any and the all take their reference from that us. He is not describing a divine wish frustrated by the creature; he is telling a waiting church why her Lord has not yet come, and the answer is that the full number is not yet gathered. Read as a universal saving intention, the verse proves too much: a God not willing that any should perish, who nonetheless delays until many do, would be either weak or unserious, and Peter's whole letter says He is neither.

What the verse does establish, and what must not be surrendered in defending it, is the genuineness of God's patience and the sincerity of the gospel call. The LORD has no pleasure in the death of the wicked; the offer of Christ to all who hear is real and is to be pressed on every man; and the delay is mercy, not indifference. The Reformed tradition has never needed to soften either half. The decree of election and the free offer of the gospel stand together, and 2 Peter 3:9 is one of the places where the patience behind both is stated in a single breath.
roots_summary: Greek bradutes (G1022), slowness; braduno (G1019), to delay; makrothumeo (G3114), to be longsuffering.
roots_lines: Greek bradutes (G1022) — slowness, tardiness; used once, in the accusation men bring against God.
Greek braduno (G1019) — to be slow, to tarry; the Lord is not slack.
Greek makrothumeo (G3114) — to be longsuffering, literally long-tempered; what the delay actually is.
Greek metanoia (G3341) — repentance, a change of mind; the end the longsuffering serves.
Hebrew remiyah (H7423) — slackness, deceit; the slack hand of Proverbs 10:4.

“account that the longsuffering of our Lord is salvation” — the interval has a purpose.
“He becometh poor that dealeth with a slack hand” — the word turned on the creature.

pos: adj. (diligent in labour; said of Jeroboam, whose industry earned him a promotion he turned into a rebellion)
etymology: From Latin industrius, diligent. At 1 Kings 11:28 it renders a Hebrew phrase meaning a doer of work — a man who gets things done.
biblical_def:
The verse is a character note dropped into the account of Solomon's decline: And the man Jeroboam was a mighty man of valour: and Solomon seeing the young man that he was industrious, he made him ruler over all the charge of the house of Joseph. The Hebrew says simply that he was a doer of work, and it is a compliment; Solomon, who wrote that a man diligent in his business shall stand before kings, saw such a man and promoted him. The proverb was fulfilled and the kingdom was torn in two by the man it was fulfilled in.

That is the hard edge of this word and the reason it deserves an entry. Industry is a real virtue, commanded repeatedly — whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might; not slothful in business; fervent in spirit; serving the Lord; whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men. But it is a virtue of the hands, and Scripture never treats it as evidence about the heart. Jeroboam was industrious, capable, and valiant, and he lifted up his hand against the king, made two calves of gold, and became the man by whose name every subsequent apostasy in the northern kingdom is measured: he walked in the way of Jeroboam, and in his sin wherewith he made Israel to sin. The last clause of Colossians 3:23 is the one that separates the two kinds of industry: as to the Lord, and not unto men.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): diligent in business or study; constantly, regularly or habitually occupied in useful labor.
webster_full: INDUSTRIOUS, a. Diligent in business or study; constantly, regularly or habitually occupied in business.
INDUSTRY, n. Habitual diligence in any employment, either bodily or mental; steady attention to business.
DILIGENT, a. Steady in application to business; constant in effort to accomplish what is undertaken.
VALOUR, n. Strength of mind in regard to danger; that quality which enables a man to encounter danger with firmness.
CHARGE, n. That which is committed to the care or management of another; trust.
scriptures: 1 Kings 11:28
And the man Jeroboam was a mighty man of valour: and Solomon seeing the young man that he was industrious, he made him ruler over all the charge of the house of Joseph.
Proverbs 22:29
Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings; he shall not stand before mean men.
Ecclesiastes 9:10
Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might; for there is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in the grave, whither thou goest.
Colossians 3:23
And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men;
corruption_summary: Capability is taken as evidence of character, and churches keep promoting the industrious man because the work gets done, exactly as Solomon did.
corruption_paragraphs: Jeroboam is the standing warning against confusing competence with godliness, and the warning is aimed at those doing the promoting. Solomon was the wisest man alive and he read the same signals any of us would: valour, energy, results. Nothing he saw was false. What he could not see from the work rate was the heart, and the New Testament therefore builds a different set of tests into the qualifications for office — blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, not greedy of filthy lucre, not a novice, one that ruleth well his own house, of good report of them which are without. Not one of them measures output.

The corresponding error is a suspicion of hard work, as if diligence were somehow carnal. Scripture will not have it. The industrious man is commended in Proverbs, the idle rebuked by Paul, and the believer told to do everything with his might and heartily. The qualifier that settles which kind of industry a man has is Colossians 3:23 — as to the Lord, and not unto men. Jeroboam worked for Solomon and then for himself; the Christian workman labours for an audience of One, and that is what keeps competence from becoming a ladder.
roots_summary: Hebrew oseh melakah (H6213 / H4399), a doer of work; charuts (H2742), diligent, sharp; Greek spoude (G4710), diligence.
roots_lines: Hebrew oseh melakah (H6213, H4399) — a doer of work; the phrase the AV renders industrious.
Hebrew charuts (H2742) — sharp, and so diligent; the diligent hand of Proverbs that maketh rich.
Hebrew gibbor chayil (H1368, H2428) — a mighty man of valour; Jeroboam's other commendation.
Greek spoude (G4710) — haste, earnestness, diligence; Romans 12:11, not slothful in business.
Greek ek psuches (G1537, G5590) — from the soul; the AV's heartily at Colossians 3:23.
usage: “Solomon seeing the young man that he was industrious” — a true observation, wrongly trusted.
“a man diligent in his business... shall stand before kings” — the proverb fulfilled, and the kingdom torn.
“as to the Lord, and not unto men” — the clause that separates two industries.

pos: n. (regular occupation; in Ezekiel 39, men set apart to the continual work of cleansing the land)
etymology: From Old French emploier, from Latin implicare, to involve or enfold. At Ezekiel 39:14 it renders a Hebrew phrase meaning men of continuance — men kept at one task without interruption.
biblical_def:
The word appears in one of the strangest assignments in Scripture: And they shall sever out men of continual employment, passing through the land to bury with the passengers those that remain upon the face of the earth, to cleanse it: after the end of seven months shall they search. After the overthrow of Gog, a permanent detail is appointed. Their whole occupation is to walk the land, mark what the general burial missed, and see it buried. Seven months of common labour first, and then a standing crew of specialists whose entire employment is the last of the cleansing.

It is an unglamorous picture of a necessary work, and that is its value. The land could not be clean while anything remained, and the search went on after the crowds had gone home. Scripture has a good deal of time for such callings. Paul tells the Thessalonians to study to be quiet, and to do your own business, and to work with your own hands — an ambition of a kind almost nobody preaches. And he calls the whole Christian life by a word taken from employment: walk worthy of the vocation wherewith ye are called. Vocation is a calling, and calling is the Reformation's recovery of the truth that the man at the bench and the man in the pulpit are both employed by the same Master and answerable to Him for the same thing — faithfulness in the post assigned.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): business; the occupation, employment or work in which a person is engaged.
webster_full: EMPLOYMENT, n. The act of employing; occupation; business; that which engages the head or hands.
EMPLOY, v.t. To occupy the time, attention and labor of; to keep busy or at work.
OCCUPATION, n. The business in which a man engages, either casually or as the stated business of his life; employment.
VOCATION, n. Employment; calling; occupation; trade; also, a summons; a call.
CLEANSE, v.t. To purify; to free from filth or foul matter; to remove pollution.
scriptures: Ezekiel 39:14

And they shall sever out men of continual employment, passing through the land to bury with the passengers those that remain upon the face of the earth, to cleanse it: after the end of seven months shall they search.
Ezekiel 39:12
And seven months shall the house of Israel be burying of them, that they may cleanse the land.
1 Thessalonians 4:11
And that ye study to be quiet, and to do your own business, and to work with your own hands, as we commanded you;
Ephesians 4:1
I therefore, the prisoner of the Lord, beseech you that ye walk worthy of the vocation wherewith ye are called,
corruption_summary: Work is either idolized as identity or dismissed as what pays for real life, and the Reformation doctrine of vocation — which is neither — goes unpreached.
corruption_paragraphs: Two opposite errors have the modern Christian worker between them. The first makes employment the whole of a man's identity, so that unemployment or retirement is a kind of death and the question what do you do? is really the question who are you? The second treats the job as spiritually irrelevant — forty hours of nothing that funds the evenings and weekends when the real living happens. The Reformers cut between both by insisting that a station is a calling: a man is put in his post by God, is to serve his neighbour there, and is judged by faithfulness in it, not by its visibility.

There is no significant progressive redefinition of this word to rebut. The principle to recover is Paul's most unfashionable ambition, stated to the Thessalonians as a command: study to be quiet, and to do your own business, and to work with your own hands. Study — make it your aim, exert yourself — to be quiet. Ezekiel's men of continual employment walked a field burying what the crowds had missed, and Scripture troubled to record them. A great deal of the work God assigns is like that, and the men who do it faithfully are not a lower order of servant.
roots_summary: Hebrew anshe tamid (H582 / H8548), men of continuance; Greek klesis (G2821), a calling; ergazomai (G2038), to work.
roots_lines: Hebrew tamid (H8548) — continual, perpetual; the same word used of the daily sacrifice and the shewbread.
Hebrew taher (H2891) — to cleanse, to make ceremonially pure; the end of the burial detail.
Greek klesis (G2821) — a calling, an invitation; rendered vocation at Ephesians 4:1.
Greek ergazomai (G2038) — to work, to labour; work with your own hands.
Greek philotimeomai (G5389) — to make it one's ambition; the verb behind study to be quiet.
usage: “men of continual employment” — a standing detail for the last of the work.
“study to be quiet, and to do your own business” — the least fashionable ambition in Paul.
“walk worthy of the vocation wherewith ye are called” — the whole life as a post.

pos: n. (an undertaking; in Job 5:12, the scheme of the crafty that their hands cannot perform)
etymology: From Old French entreprise, an undertaking, from entreprendre, to take in hand. At Job 5:12 it renders Hebrew tushiyyah, sound wisdom or enterprise — here the crafty man's successful plan, defeated.
biblical_def:
Eliphaz is not always wrong, and this is one of the places where his theology is sound even though his application to Job is not: He disappointeth the devices of the crafty, so that their hands cannot perform their enterprise. The verb is exact. God does not merely disapprove of the schemes of the crafty; He disappoints them — breaks them off at the point of execution, so that the hands cannot perform what the mind conceived. The next verse presses it further: He taketh the wise in their own craftiness: and the counsel of the froward is carried headlong. The trap is not sprung from outside; the cleverness itself is the snare.

Scripture returns to this again and again, and always with the same two halves. There are many devices in a man's heart; nevertheless the counsel of the LORD, that shall stand. The LORD bringeth the counsel of the heathen to nought: he maketh the devices of the people of none effect. Haman built the gallows; Ahithophel's counsel was turned to foolishness; the chief priests sealed the stone and set a watch. In every case the enterprise was competent, and in every case the competence served the purpose it was designed to defeat. This is not fatalism — men really plan, and are really answerable for what they plan — but it is the doctrine that God governs every enterprise, including the ones raised against Him, and that His counsel is the one that stands.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): that which is undertaken; an attempt; an arduous or hazardous undertaking.
webster_full: ENTERPRISE, n. That which is undertaken, or attempted to be performed; an attempt; an undertaking of hazard.
DEVICE, n. That which is formed by design; a scheme formed by the mind; a contrivance; a stratagem.
CRAFTY, a. Cunning; artful; skilful in devising and pursuing a scheme, by deceiving others.
DISAPPOINT, v.t. To defeat of expectation, wish, hope, desire or intention; to frustrate; to balk.
FROWARD, a. Perverse; that is, turning from with displeasure; not willing to yield or comply.
scriptures: Job 5:12
He disappointeth the devices of the crafty, so that their hands cannot perform their enterprise.
Job 5:13
He taketh the wise in their own craftiness: and the counsel of the froward is carried headlong.
Proverbs 19:21
There are many devices in a man's heart; nevertheless the counsel of the LORD, that shall stand.
Psalm 33:10
The LORD bringeth the counsel of the heathen to nought: he maketh the devices of the people of none effect.
corruption_summary: History is read as the sum of human planning, and the doctrine that God governs the enterprises of men — including those raised against Him — is treated as a pious flourish rather than a fact.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern account of events is a story of forces and actors, and God appears in it, if at all, as a sentiment held by some of the participants. Scripture's account is different at the root. The devices of the crafty are real devices, formed by real minds, and they are disappointed — the hands cannot perform them — by a God who is not one of the actors but the author. Paul quotes Job 5:13 directly in 1 Corinthians, which settles that this is not merely Eliphaz's opinion but revealed truth, however badly the speaker applied it to the man on the ash heap.

The doctrine cuts two ways, and both are needed. To the believer watching competent wickedness prosper, it is the promise that the counsel of the LORD shall stand and that the cleverness now winning is the material of its own undoing. To the believer making plans, it is a warning against the enterprise conceived without reference to God — the very thing James rebukes: ye ought to say, If the Lord will, we shall live, and do this, or that. Neither passage forbids planning. Both forbid planning as though the outcome belonged to the planner.
roots_summary: Hebrew tushiyyah (H8454), sound wisdom, enterprise; machashabah (H4284), a device or plan; parar (H6565), to break, to frustrate.
roots_lines: Hebrew tushiyyah (H8454) — sound wisdom, and so an able undertaking; rendered enterprise.
Hebrew machashabah (H4284) — a thought, a device, a plan; the schemes of the crafty.
Hebrew parar (H6565) — to break, to make void; the verb behind disappointeth.
Hebrew arum (H6175) — crafty, subtle; the same adjective used of the serpent in Genesis 3.
Hebrew etsah (H6098) — counsel; the LORD's counsel, which shall stand.
usage: “their hands cannot perform their enterprise” — broken off at the point of execution.
“He taketh the wise in their own craftiness” — the cleverness is the snare.
“nevertheless the counsel of the LORD, that shall stand” — the other half of every plan.

pos: v.i. (to become surety for; Hezekiah's prayer, O LORD, I am oppressed; undertake for me)
etymology: English under + take — to take a thing upon oneself. At Isaiah 38:14 it renders Hebrew arab, to go surety, to pledge oneself for another's debt.
biblical_def:
Hezekiah is sick unto death, has been told to set his house in order, and prays. The record he wrote afterward contains the sentence: Like a crane or a swallow, so did I chatter: I did mourn as a dove: mine eyes fail with looking upward: O LORD, I am oppressed; undertake for me. The sounds he uses are the noises of small birds — chattering, mourning — a man whose prayer has been reduced to something barely articulate. And then four words that are one of the great prayers of Scripture: undertake for me.

The Hebrew is the legal word for standing surety. It is what Judah did for Benjamin before Joseph — thy servant became surety for the lad — the pledge by which one man makes another's debt his own and can be seized for it. Hezekiah is asking God to step into his case as the one who will answer for him, because he cannot answer for himself. The psalmist prays the same thing: Be surety for thy servant for good. And the New Testament answers both in a sentence about Christ: By so much was Jesus made a surety of a better testament. That is the only place in the New Testament where the word appears, and it is the whole gospel in one legal term. The Son does not merely pray for the debtor; He is the surety, and the claim comes to Him.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): to take upon one's self; to engage in; to become surety or bail for another.
webster_full: UNDERTAKE, v.t. To engage in; to enter upon; to take in hand; to become bound to perform.
UNDERTAKE, v.i. To become a surety; to be bound for another; to promise.
SURETY, n. One that is bound with and for another; one who enters into a bond or recognizance to answer for another's debt.
OPPRESSED, pp. Burdened with unreasonable impositions; overpowered; heavily burdened.
CRANE, n. A migratory fowl of the genus Ardea, with long legs and neck.
scriptures: Isaiah 38:14
Like a crane or a swallow, so did I chatter: I did mourn as a dove: mine eyes fail with looking upward: O LORD, I am oppressed; undertake for me.
Isaiah 38:15
What shall I say? he hath both spoken unto me, and himself hath done it: I shall go softly all my years in the bitterness of my soul.
Psalm 119:122
Be surety for thy servant for good: let not the proud oppress me.
Hebrews 7:22
By so much was Jesus made a surety of a better testament.
corruption_summary: Prayer is taught as a technique with conditions attached, when Hezekiah's is barely articulate and God answers the four words a dying man could still manage.
corruption_paragraphs: A great deal of teaching about prayer amounts to instruction in how to get it right — the posture, the formula, the sufficient faith, the absence of doubt. Isaiah 38 is a standing rebuke to all of it. The king's own description of his praying is that he chattered like a swallow and mourned like a dove, and that his eyes failed with looking upward. That is a man at the end of his articulacy. What he had left was four words of legal Hebrew, and they were enough, because the power of prayer has never been in the praying. Paul says the Spirit helpeth our infirmities, for we know not what we should pray for as we ought, and makes intercession with groanings which cannot be uttered.

The second thing to hold is what the word became. Hezekiah asked God to be his surety and was given fifteen years; the church has been given the Surety Himself. By so much was Jesus made a surety of a better testament — the only use of the word in the New Testament, and it is a person, not a favour. A surety is liable. The claim that would have fallen on the debtor falls on him, and he pays it. That is why a believer's worst prayer still gets through, and it has nothing to do with the quality of the chattering.
roots_summary: Hebrew arab (H6148), to pledge, to become surety; ashaq (H6234), oppression; Greek egguos (G1450), a surety.
roots_lines: Hebrew arab (H6148) — to give a pledge, to become surety; Judah's word for himself before Joseph.
Hebrew oshqah (H6234) — oppression, a burden; I am oppressed.
Greek egguos (G1450) — a surety, a guarantor; used once, of the Lord Jesus in Hebrews 7:22.
Hebrew sus (H5483) — rendered crane; one of the two birds whose sound Hezekiah's prayer resembled.
Hebrew dalal (H1809) — to hang down, to fail; mine eyes fail with looking upward.
usage: “O LORD, I am oppressed; undertake for me” — four words from a dying king.
“Be surety for thy servant for good” — the same prayer in the Psalter.
“Jesus made a surety of a better testament” — the answer, and it is a Person.

pos: n. (toil to the point of pain; in Paul's catalogue of what the apostleship cost him)
etymology: From Old French peine, from Latin poena, a penalty. At 2 Corinthians 11:27 it renders Greek mochthos, hard and wearying labour — toil that hurts, distinguished from kopos, weariness.
biblical_def:
Paul is forced by the false apostles at Corinth into a reluctant boast, and what he boasts of is the bill: In weariness and painfulness, in watchings often, in hunger and thirst, in fastings often, in cold and nakedness. Two Greek words open the list and they are not synonyms. Kopos is the weariness that follows labour; mochthos is the hardship in the labour itself, toil that hurts while it is being done. Paul has already given the prisons, the stripes, the shipwrecks, the night and a day in the deep; he now gives the ordinary grinding cost — sleepless nights, no food, no coat.

And then, having listed all of it, he says that the real weight is something else entirely: Beside those things that are without, that which cometh upon me daily, the care of all the churches. The stripes are the outside. The daily pressure of anxiety for congregations he could not reach is the thing he names last and heaviest. Any pastor who has lain awake over a church he cannot fix knows why. The chapter that follows gives the answer that governs the whole catalogue and it is not relief but sufficiency: My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. Paul does not get the thorn removed. He gets a sentence, and on the strength of it he says he will glory in infirmities.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the quality of giving pain; laboriousness; toil; the state of being laborious to a degree of suffering.
webster_full: PAINFULNESS, n. Affliction; sorrow; grief; laboriousness; the quality of being painful or toilsome.
PAINFUL, a. Giving pain; distressing; also, requiring labor or toil; difficult; executed with laborious effort.
WEARINESS, n. The state of being weary or tired; lassitude; that lassitude which is induced by labor.
WATCHING, n. Vigilance; forbearance of sleep; wakefulness; attendance without sleep.
INFIRMITY, n. An unsound or unhealthy state of the body; weakness; feebleness.
scriptures: 2 Corinthians 11:27
In weariness and painfulness, in watchings often, in hunger and thirst, in fastings often, in cold and nakedness.
2 Corinthians 11:28
Beside those things that are without, that which cometh upon me daily, the care of all the churches.
2 Corinthians 12:9

And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me.
Galatians 6:9
And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not.
corruption_summary: Ministry is sold as fulfilment, and the apostolic job description — weariness, painfulness, watchings, hunger, cold, and the daily care of the churches — is quietly never read aloud to candidates.
corruption_paragraphs: The picture of gospel work now circulating is influence, platform and impact, and the men recruited on that picture are the ones who break first. Paul's own summary of his credentials is a list of costs, and he offers it with embarrassment, under compulsion from opponents who were boasting of better things. The Reformed tradition has generally been honest about this; the Puritans wrote about the ministry as a burden a man should not seek unless he cannot escape it, and Baxter's Reformed Pastor assumes a labour that will shorten a life. A church that will not say this to its young men is not protecting them.

The other half must be said as firmly. Paul is not commending misery, and there is a species of ministerial self-pity that quotes 2 Corinthians 11 as a way of demanding sympathy. What follows in chapter 12 rules it out: the thorn stays, the grace is sufficient, and the apostle says he takes pleasure in infirmities for Christ's sake. The cost is real and the compensation is not a lighter load but the power of Christ resting on a man. Galatians adds the timetable: in due season we shall reap, if we faint not — not now, and not never.
roots_summary: Greek mochthos (G3449), painful toil; kopos (G2873), weariness from labour; agrupnia (G70), sleeplessness; merimna (G3308), anxious care.
roots_lines: Greek mochthos (G3449) — hard and painful labour; used three times, always by Paul, always of his own work.
Greek kopos (G2873) — a beating, and so weariness from toil; the first word of the pair.
Greek agrupnia (G70) — sleeplessness, watchings; nights spent awake.
Greek merimna (G3308) — anxious care; the daily weight of all the churches.
Greek arkeo (G714) — to be sufficient; my grace is sufficient for thee.
usage: “In weariness and painfulness, in watchings often” — the apostolic bill.
“that which cometh upon me daily, the care of all the churches” — named last and heaviest.
“My grace is sufficient for thee” — not relief, but sufficiency.

pos: adj. (tiring; of the nights appointed to Job, which would not pass)
etymology: From weary, Old English werig, tired. At Job 7:3 it renders a Hebrew phrase meaning nights of trouble — nights assigned, numbered out, and endured.
biblical_def:
Job is answering Eliphaz, and the sentence is one of the most exact descriptions of suffering in Scripture: So am I made to possess months of vanity, and wearisome nights are appointed to me. Two verbs do the work. He is made to possess the empty months — they are given to him as a holding, an inheritance — and the nights are appointed, numbered out and assigned. Job never says his affliction is random. He says it is allotted, and that is precisely why he takes his complaint to the One who allotted it.

The next verse gives the texture: When I lie down, I say, When shall I arise, and the night be gone? and I am full of tossings to and fro unto the dawning of the day. Anyone who has lain awake in trouble recognizes the arithmetic of that sentence, the clock-watching, the night that will not move. Scripture lets it stand without hurrying to comfort. Ecclesiastes has the same weariness in a different key — All things are full of labour; man cannot utter it: the eye is not satisfied with seeing — and Malachi records the other kind, the weariness of men bored with the worship of God: Behold, what a weariness is it! and ye have snuffed at it. One weariness is affliction honestly borne; the other is contempt dressed as fatigue. The Bible is tender with the first and merciless with the second.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): causing weariness; tiresome; tedious; fatiguing to the body or mind.
webster_full: WEARISOME, a. Causing weariness; tiresome; tedious; fatiguing; irksome.
WEARY, a. Having the strength much exhausted by toil or violent exertion; tired; fatigued.
TEDIOUS, a. Wearisome; tiresome from continuance, prolixity, or slowness.

APPOINT, v.t. To fix; to ordain; to constitute; to allot, assign or designate.
scriptures: Job 7:3
So am I made to possess months of vanity, and wearisome nights are appointed to me.
Job 7:4
When I lie down, I say, When shall I arise, and the night be gone? and I am full of tossings to and fro unto the dawning of the day.
Ecclesiastes 1:8
All things are full of labour; man cannot utter it: the eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing.
Malachi 1:13

Ye said also, Behold, what a weariness is it! and ye have snuffed at it, saith the LORD of hosts; and ye brought that which was torn, and the lame, and the sick; thus ye brought an offering: should I accept this of your hand? saith the LORD.
corruption_summary: Complaint and lament are treated as the same thing, so that either all grief is forbidden or all grumbling is excused; Job and Malachi in the same Bible settle the difference.
corruption_paragraphs: Put Job 7 and Malachi 1 side by side and the line becomes visible. Job says the nights are wearisome and appointed, and says it to God, at length, without softening a syllable; the book ends with the LORD telling Eliphaz that Job has spoken of Him the thing that is right. The priests in Malachi say what a weariness is it about the service of God itself, snuff at the altar, and bring the torn and the lame; and the LORD asks whether He should accept it of their hand. Lament is affliction brought to God. Weariness with God is contempt, and it shows up in what a man is willing to offer.

The pastoral use of this is large. A congregation that has been taught only the Malachi half will silence its sufferers, who then grieve alone and conclude that faith has no room for them. A congregation that has been taught only the Job half will excuse a chronic grumbling that is really unbelief. What the Bible does is give the sufferer a vocabulary — whole psalms of it — while refusing to let anyone snuff at the altar. And to both it holds out the promise of an appointed end: let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not.
roots_summary: Hebrew amal (H5999), trouble, toil; yare / manah (H4487), to appoint or number out; shav (H7723), vanity, emptiness.
roots_lines: Hebrew amal (H5999) — toil, trouble, misery; the wearisome of Job's nights.
Hebrew manah (H4487) — to count, to appoint; the nights were numbered out to him.
Hebrew shav (H7723) — emptiness, vanity; the months he is made to possess.
Hebrew nadad (H5074) — to flee away, to be restless; the tossings to and fro until dawn.
Hebrew telaah (H8513) — weariness, hardship; Malachi's word on the priests' lips.

“When shall I arise, and the night be gone?” — the arithmetic of a sleepless bed.
“Behold, what a weariness is it!” — the other weariness, and its offering.

pos: adj. (occupied; in 1 Kings 20:40, the excuse of the man who lost his prisoner)
etymology: From Old English bisig, careful or anxious. At 1 Kings 20:40 it renders a Hebrew verb meaning to be occupied or engaged — the prophet's word in a parable aimed at Ahab.
biblical_def:
A prophet in disguise stops Ahab on the road with a story. He had been given a prisoner to guard on pain of his own life, and he lost him: And as thy servant was busy here and there, he was gone. And the king of Israel said unto him, So shall thy judgment be; thyself hast decided it. Ahab passes sentence instantly, because the case is obvious. Then the prophet takes off the ashes from his face and the king discovers he has just sentenced himself for letting Benhadad go.

The excuse is the point, and it is one of the most quoted phrases in Scripture outside its own context because everyone recognizes it. Busy here and there. Not idle, not asleep, not disobedient in any way he could name — occupied. He had been given one charge and he was doing five other things, and the one charge walked away while he worked. Nothing in the parable suggests the here-and-there was wicked. That is precisely what makes it damning, and it is why the phrase has always had a special sting for men in ministry and in families. The New Testament has a hard word for a related failure — those who walk disorderly, working not at all, but are busybodies — a pun in the Greek as in the English, men busy about everything but their own business. Scripture treats occupation as no defence at all when the thing entrusted has been lost.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): employed with constant attention; engaged in business; also, officious; meddling.
webster_full: BUSY, a. Employed with constant attention; engaged about something that renders interruption inconvenient.
BUSY, a. Officious; meddling; engaged in affairs not one's own.
BUSYBODY, n. One who meddles with the concerns of others; a vain, officious meddler.
CHARGE, n. That which is committed to the care of another; trust; custody.
DISORDERLY, adv. In a disorderly manner; without law or order; irregularly.
scriptures: 1 Kings 20:40
And as thy servant was busy here and there, he was gone. And the king of Israel said unto him, So shall thy judgment be; thyself hast decided it.
1 Kings 20:39

And as the king passed by, he cried unto the king: and he said, Thy servant went out into the midst of the battle; and, behold, a man turned aside, and brought a man unto me, and said, Keep this man: if by any means he be missing, then shall thy life be for his life, or else thou shalt pay a talent of silver.
2 Thessalonians 3:11
For we hear that there are some which walk among you disorderly, working not at all, but are busybodies.
1 Timothy 5:13
And withal they learn to be idle, wandering about from house to house; and not only idle, but tattlers also and busybodies, speaking things which they ought not.
corruption_summary: Busyness is worn as a credential, and a life that could not name the one thing entrusted to it passes for a faithful one because the calendar is full.
corruption_paragraphs: Busy here and there is the epitaph of a great many respectable lives. The man in the parable has no scandal to confess. He was occupied, probably usefully, and the charge he had been given walked off while he was occupied. Fathers lose children that way; pastors lose congregations that way; and nobody at any point does anything a court would call wrong. Ahab's verdict is instant because the case is plain when it is somebody else's: thyself hast decided it. The parable is constructed to get the judgment out of the hearer before he knows he is the defendant, exactly as Nathan did with David.

Paul adds the sharper form of the failure. The disorderly at Thessalonica were working not at all, but are busybodies — a wordplay that survives translation: not busy, but busybodies, energetic about everyone's business except their own. His remedy is severe and practical: if any would not work, neither should he eat, and then, that with quietness they work, and eat their own bread. The cure for the wrong kind of busyness is not more rest but the right work — knowing what has been committed to you and being found with it when the Master comes.
roots_summary: Hebrew asah / hayah in the idiom busy here and there; Greek periergazomai (G4020), to be a busybody; ataktos (G814), disorderly.
roots_lines: Hebrew asah hennah wahennah — doing this way and that; the idiom the AV renders busy here and there.
Greek periergazomai (G4020) — to work round about, to meddle; the busybody of 2 Thessalonians 3:11.
Greek ataktos (G814) — out of rank, disorderly; a military word for a man out of his place.
Greek hesuchia (G2271) — quietness; the manner Paul prescribes for working and eating one's own bread.
Greek phluaros (G5397) — a tattler, a prater; the busybody's companion vice in 1 Timothy 5:13.
usage: “as thy servant was busy here and there, he was gone” — the excuse that is the indictment.
“thyself hast decided it” — the verdict pronounced before the defendant knew.
“working not at all, but are busybodies” — the pun Paul made in Greek.

pos: v. (risked; of Barnabas and Paul, men who hazarded their lives for the name of the Lord Jesus)
etymology: From Old French hasard, a game of chance, ultimately from Arabic az-zahr, the die. At Acts 15:26 it renders Greek paradidomi, to hand over — men who had handed their lives across for the Name.
biblical_def:
The letter from the Jerusalem council carries a line of commendation that its writers did not have to include: Men that have hazarded their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. It is said of Barnabas and Paul, and the reason it is there matters. The council had just settled the hardest question the early church faced — whether Gentile converts must be circumcised — and the two men carrying the verdict back to Antioch were the ones who had done the disputed work. The apostles and elders put their reputations behind them in a sentence, and the sentence is about risk taken for a Name.

The Greek is stronger than hazarded suggests: they had handed their lives over, given them across, the same verb used of Christ being delivered up. Paul had been stoned at Lystra and dragged out of the city for dead, and had gone back in the next day. The New Testament keeps a short list of such men. Priscilla and Aquila have for my life laid down their own necks; Epaphroditus for the work of Christ he was nigh unto death, not regarding his life, to supply your lack of service toward me. The Old Testament has the same commendation for Gideon — my father fought for you, and adventured his life far — and for David, who did put his life in his hand, and slew the Philistine. In every case the risk is for others and for the Name, never for the thrill of it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): exposed to peril; risked; put in danger of loss or injury.
webster_full: HAZARDED, pp. Exposed to danger or loss; risked; ventured.
HAZARD, v.t. To expose to chance; to put in danger of loss or injury; to venture; to risk.
PERIL, n. Danger; risk; hazard; jeopardy; exposure of person or property to injury or destruction.
VENTURE, v.t. To expose to hazard; to risk; to put or send on a venture.
NAME, n. That by which a person or thing is called; also, reputation; character; renown.
scriptures: Acts 15:26
Men that have hazarded their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.
Acts 15:25
It seemed good unto us, being assembled with one accord, to send chosen men unto you with our beloved Barnabas and Paul,
Romans 16:4
Who have for my life laid down their own necks: unto whom not only I give thanks, but also all the churches of the Gentiles.
Philippians 2:30
Because for the work of Christ he was nigh unto death, not regarding his life, to supply your lack of service toward me.
corruption_summary: Risk for the gospel is romanticized at a distance and avoided at home, while the New Testament commends men who took it for other people's benefit and never for their own reputation.
corruption_paragraphs: Two failures attach to this word. The first is the sentimental one: admiring the missionary story while arranging a Christian life from which every cost has been engineered out. The second is its mirror, a recklessness that courts danger for the standing it confers — and the New Testament's commendations rule it out, because every man on the list hazarded his life for somebody. Priscilla and Aquila laid down their necks for Paul's life. Epaphroditus came near death to supply what the Philippians could not deliver themselves. Barnabas and Paul risked theirs for the Name. None of them is praised for having been in danger.

There is no significant progressive redefinition here to rebut. The principle to recover is that the church is meant to say such things out loud about her own. The Jerusalem council, in a formal letter settling a doctrinal controversy, stopped to commend two men by name for what their faithfulness had cost them. Congregations are often better at scrutinizing their workers than at honouring them, and Scripture does both — Paul names Diotrephes and he names Epaphroditus, and he tells the Philippians to hold such in reputation.
roots_summary: Greek paradidomi (G3860), to hand over, to deliver up; paraboleuomai (G3851), to expose oneself to danger; psuche (G5590), life or soul.

Greek paraboleuomai (G3851) — to throw alongside, to gamble; Epaphroditus not regarding his life.
Greek psuche (G5590) — life, soul; what these men handed across.
Greek trachelos (G5137) — the neck; Priscilla and Aquila laid down their own.
Greek onoma (G3686) — name; the Name for which the risk was taken.
usage: “Men that have hazarded their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ” — a council's commendation.
“Who have for my life laid down their own necks” — risk taken for a person.
“not regarding his life, to supply your lack of service” — Epaphroditus' errand.

pos: v. (risked, ventured; of Gideon, who adventured his life far and was repaid by the murder of his sons)
etymology: From Old French aventure, from Latin adventurus, about to happen. At Judges 9:17 it renders Hebrew shalak, to cast or fling — literally, he flung his life out in front of him.
biblical_def:
Jotham is standing on the top of mount Gerizim shouting down at the men of Shechem who have just crowned his half-brother Abimelech after murdering seventy of his brothers on one stone. He reminds them what their king's father did for them: For my father fought for you, and adventured his life far, and delivered you out of the hand of Midian. The Hebrew verb is the one for casting or flinging — Gideon threw his life out ahead of him, three hundred men against a host lying along the valley like grasshoppers for multitude. And this is what the men of Shechem paid back.

The word describes the same virtue Acts commends in Barnabas and Paul, and Judges 9 supplies the other half of the picture: risk taken faithfully is not always met with gratitude, and often the reckoning comes a generation late. David did put his life in his hand, and slew the Philistine, and the LORD wrought a great salvation for all Israel, and Jonathan has to remind Saul of it while Saul is trying to kill him. Jotham's parable of the trees ends in a curse that took three years to come true, and it came true exactly. The believer who has adventured something for God and been ill repaid is in old company, and the book of Judges does not tell him the accounting has been cancelled — only that it is not his to make.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): risked; hazarded; ventured; exposed to danger or loss.
webster_full: ADVENTURED, pp. Risked; hazarded; put to hazard.
ADVENTURE, v.t. To risk or hazard; to venture; to dare.
DELIVER, v.t. To free; to release, as from restraint; to set at liberty; to rescue.
REQUITE, v.t. To repay; to return an equivalent, in a good or bad sense.
PARABLE, n. A fable or allegorical relation or representation of something real in life or nature.
scriptures: Judges 9:17
(For my father fought for you, and adventured his life far, and delivered you out of the hand of Midian:
1 Samuel 19:5

For he did put his life in his hand, and slew the Philistine, and the LORD wrought a great salvation for all Israel: thou sawest it, and didst rejoice: wherefore then wilt thou sin against innocent blood, to slay David without a cause?
Acts 15:26
Men that have hazarded their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.
Philippians 2:30
Because for the work of Christ he was nigh unto death, not regarding his life, to supply your lack of service toward me.
corruption_summary: Faithful risk is expected to be rewarded in this life, and when it is not, the believer concludes that God did not see it; Judges 9 says the accounting is real and slow.
corruption_paragraphs: Jotham's speech is the sharpest statement in Scripture of a grievance every generation feels: a man spent himself for people who forgot it and then destroyed his house. The chapter does not answer with sentiment. It answers with a verdict — God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the men of Shechem — and with an account settled three years later, when a woman cast a piece of millstone from a tower and broke Abimelech's skull. The narrator states the theology plainly: Thus God rendered the wickedness of Abimelech, which he did unto his father, in slaying his seventy brethren.

The pastoral use is not vindictiveness but patience. A believer who has adventured something real — a reputation, a livelihood, a friendship — and watched it go unacknowledged is tempted to conclude either that the risk was foolish or that God was inattentive. Judges 9 rules out both. The accounting is real, it is God's, and its timing is not the aggrieved man's to set. Paul says the same in a quieter key: let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not. Due season is His word, not ours.
roots_summary: Hebrew shalak (H7993), to cast or fling; nephesh (H5315), life, soul; yasha (H3467), to deliver or save.
roots_lines: Hebrew shalak (H7993) — to cast, to fling; Gideon flung his life out before him.
Hebrew nephesh (H5315) — life, soul, the living self; what was cast.
Hebrew yasha (H3467) — to save, to deliver; what the adventure accomplished for Shechem.
Hebrew gamal (H1580) — to deal out, to requite; the verb of God's rendering to Abimelech.
Hebrew mashal (H4912) — a parable; the form of Jotham's speech about the trees.
usage: “my father fought for you, and adventured his life far” — the debt Shechem forgot.
“he did put his life in his hand, and slew the Philistine” — Jonathan reminding Saul.
“in due season we shall reap, if we faint not” — the timing that is not ours.
